gloss_terse: To put, place, or set; by extension to make into, appoint, direct attention, or bestow (name, attribute)
gloss_readable: One of Hebrew's most versatile verbs, sin/sim covers the full arc from physically placing an object to transforming reality itself. A shepherd puts a bundle on a donkey (Gen 22:6), but God 'puts' Abraham's seed as the dust of the earth (Gen 13:16) — the same verb now meaning 'make into.' Pharaoh 'sets' Joseph over Egypt (Gen 41:33), and the prophets urge Israel to 'set heart' upon God's ways. Across all 43 languages the translations consistently split along these lines: French mettre, Spanish poner, and German setzen/legen for physical placement, but faire/hacer/machen when transformation is meant.

senses.1: The concrete core: placing or setting an object physically in a location. This dominates usage (444x) and is confirmed by consistent translation as 'put/place' across all target languages — French mettre, Spanish poner, German legte/setzte. Gen 22:6 (Abraham placing wood on Isaac) and Gen 28:11 (Jacob setting a stone under his head) are paradigmatic.
senses.2: A transformative extension (91x): making or turning someone/something into a new state. Where sense 1 moves an object spatially, this sense changes identity. French shifts from mettre to placer/faire, Spanish from poner to hacer. God's promise to 'make' Abraham's seed as the sand (Gen 13:16) or 'make' the bitter waters sweet (Exod 15:25) illustrate this.
senses.3: To appoint or install a person in a role of authority (23x). The object is always personal — a taskmaster (Exod 1:11), a judge (Exod 2:14), military officers (Exod 18:21). Spanish Pusieron and French désigna confirm the administrative nuance distinct from physical placement.
senses.4: Idiomatic: to 'set the heart/mind' upon something, meaning to pay attention, consider, or take notice (13x). The collocation sim lev is a fixed phrase. German setzte (reflexive attention) and French fit preserve the metaphor of placing one's inner faculty upon a matter (1Sam 8:11–12, Exod 14:21).
senses.5: An extended sense of giving, bestowing, or assigning (3x) — particularly a name or attribute. French donner and German geben replace the placement verbs entirely, confirming a genuinely distinct semantic field. Num 6:26 (granting peace) and Josh 7:19 (giving glory) are key passages.
senses.6: A single occurrence at Job 38:33 where God asks Job whether he can 'establish' or 'set' the ordinances of the heavens. English 'establish' and Spanish poner suggest a cosmic-regulatory sense bridging placement and decree. Best understood as a rhetorical extension of sense 1 into cosmological order.
senses.7: Gen 47:6: Pharaoh tells Joseph to 'set them' (his family) in the best of the land — combining physical placement with appointment-like authorization. The demonstrative 'them' and the administrative context make this a borderline case between senses 1 and 3.
senses.8: Ps 66:9: 'The One who sets our soul in life' — a participial form describing God's sustaining action. French le nom notwithstanding, the Hebrew sense is preserving or keeping alive, an extended metaphorical placement into the domain of life.
senses.9: Job 4:20: 'Without anyone noticing' — the sense of paying attention or taking notice, closely related to sense 4 (set heart). Spanish ponga atención confirms the cognitive-attentive reading, though here it is negated: destruction comes without anyone 'setting mind' upon it.
senses.10: Job 38:9: 'When I made the cloud its garment' — God's creative act of wrapping the sea. English 'when I made' and Spanish Cuando puse point to a creative-transformative use closely allied with sense 2, but in the specific context of primordial creation.
senses.11: 1Chr 17:9: 'And I will appoint a place for my people Israel' — a promissory, future-oriented appointment of territory. Closely related to sense 3 (appoint) but with spatial-territorial rather than personnel focus. Spanish pondré and French mettre retain the placement metaphor.
senses.12: Ps 147:14: 'The One who makes peace your border' — a participial form describing God's action of establishing shalom as Israel's boundary condition. This combines the transformative sense (2) with the cosmic-ordering sense (6), applied to national well-being.

gloss_terse: To be firm, established; to prepare, make ready; to set right, direct; to confirm or found (Nifal/Piel/Hifil)
gloss_readable: Built on the root idea of firmness and solidity, kun spans the arc from passive stability to active preparation. In Nifal, a throne 'is established' forever (2Sam 7:16); in Hifil, a host 'prepares' a meal (Gen 43:16) or God 'establishes' a kingdom (2Sam 5:12). The Piel intensifies: God 'founded' the earth (Deut 32:6) or 'confirmed' a people (2Sam 7:24). Arabic kana ('exist, be') and Ethiopic kona ('be') preserve the stative core, while Aramaic kawwen ('put right, correct') captures the active sense that Hebrew develops so richly.

senses.1: Hifil causative: to prepare, make ready, or provide in advance (80x). The most frequent sense, confirmed by Spanish preparé/había-preparado and German bereitete. Gen 43:16 (Joseph ordering a meal prepared) and Josh 1:11 (preparing provisions for crossing the Jordan) are paradigmatic. Arabic a'adda mirrors this causative preparation.
senses.2: Nifal stative: to be established, stand firm, or endure (42x). Describes thrones, kingdoms, and divine purposes that persist through time. 2Sam 7:16 ('your throne shall be established forever') is foundational. French affermir and Spanish firme/establecido consistently render this enduring stability. Gen 41:32 confirms that a divinely repeated dream 'is established.'
senses.3: Hifil causative with establishment focus: to establish, set up, or make firm (28x). Distinct from sense 1 (preparation) in that the goal is permanence rather than readiness. God establishes David's kingdom (2Sam 5:12), Solomon's throne (1Kgs 2:24). Arabic thabbata/aqama and German gründen confirm the foundational nuance.
senses.4: Piel intensive: to establish firmly, confirm, or found (24x). The intensified middle ground between Nifal passivity and Hifil causation. God 'founded' the world (Deut 32:6), 'established' Israel as His people (2Sam 7:24). French affermir and Spanish estableciste capture the deliberate, thorough strengthening. Exod 15:17 uses it of God's sanctuary.
senses.5: Nifal participial as adjective: ready, prepared, standing by (17x). Arabic musta'idd and Swahili tayari confirm readiness rather than permanence. Exod 19:11 ('be ready by the third day') and Josh 8:4 ('be ready') exemplify this anticipatory state distinct from sense 2's enduring firmness.
senses.6: Nifal stative with epistemic force: right, certain, true, verified (9x). Arabic sawaban/yaqin and German Wahrheit distinguish this from physical firmness. Used in Deuteronomic legal contexts: Deut 13:14 and 17:4 require that a matter 'is certain' before judgment proceeds. Exod 8:26 ('the right thing') shows ethical application.
senses.7: Pual and Hofal passive: to be established, be prepared, be set in place by another agent (5x). Arabic mu'add/yuthabbatu confirms the passive construction. Ps 37:23 ('a man's steps are established by the LORD') and Isa 16:5 ('a throne shall be established in mercy') are key passages showing divine agency behind the passive.
senses.8: Hifil/Piel with directional force: to direct, aim, set toward a target (4x). Arabic tusawwibu ('aim') and Swahili kuelekeza ('direct') differentiate this from preparation or establishment. Ps 21:12 (aiming arrows) and Jer 10:23 ('it is not in man to direct his steps') show both literal and metaphorical directing.
senses.9: Hitpael reflexive: to establish oneself or be self-established (3x). Arabic yasta'idd/tuthabbatina indicates self-directed action. Prov 24:3 ('by wisdom a house is established') and Isa 54:14 ('in righteousness you shall be established') blend reflexive agency with divine enablement.
senses.10: At Josh 3:17 and 4:3, describing priests standing 'firm' on dry ground in the Jordan. Spanish firme and English firm point to a physical, bodily firmness — feet planted solidly — extending the stative core into a concrete, spatial sense of stable footing during the miracle of the river crossing.
senses.11: Piel with implements as object: fitting or setting arrows on the bowstring (2x). Ps 11:2 ('the wicked have fitted their arrow') and Isa 51:13 preserve the preparation sense but applied specifically to weaponry. Arabic a'addu in the context of arms preparation confirms the military-technical nuance.
senses.12: Ezek 16:7: 'Your breasts were formed' — describing physical maturation in God's allegory of Jerusalem as a girl growing up. The Nifal here means 'were shaped, developed, came into full form.' Spanish se formaron and English were-formed capture the biological development sense, unique to this passage.

gloss_terse: To be heavy or weighty; to honor, glorify; to harden; to be honored or glorious (Qal/Piel/Nifal/Hifil)
gloss_readable: At the root of kavod ('glory') lies this verb whose physical sense — sheer heaviness — grounds all its theological weight. Hands grow heavy with age (Gen 48:10), Pharaoh's heart is made heavy with stubbornness (Exod 8:15), but the same root commands children to 'honor' their parents (Exod 20:12) and calls worshippers to 'glorify' God (Ps 86:12). The semantic journey from physical mass to social honor to divine glory is mirrored across the target languages: Arabic uses karrама for honor but athqala for physical heaviness, while Korean distinguishes gongyeonghada (respect) from wangohage hada (harden).

senses.1: Piel active: to honor, show respect, esteem (30x). The central ethical sense, commanded in the Decalogue (Exod 20:12, 'Honor your father and mother'). Arabic karrама, Korean gongyeonghada, Swahili -heshimu all render the interpersonal respect. Balaam's repeated promises to 'honor' Balaam (Num 22:17, 37) show the transactional dimension.
senses.2: Qal stative: to be physically heavy, weighty, burdensome (19x). The concrete foundation of the entire semantic field. Famine is 'heavy' upon the land (Gen 18:20's outcry is 'heavy'), Jacob's eyes are 'heavy' with age (Gen 48:10), battle grows 'heavy' (Judg 20:34). Spanish agravó/endureció and French fut-lourd preserve the physical metaphor.
senses.3: Nifal participial and finite: to be honored, esteemed, noble (17x). The passive counterpart of sense 1, often substantivized as 'nobles' or 'honored ones.' Gen 34:19 (Shechem 'the most honored'), 1Sam 9:6 (the man of God 'highly honored'). French honora and Spanish honorable consistently mark social standing.
senses.4: Hifil causative: to make heavy, burden, or harden (14x). Primarily the Exodus hardening motif — Pharaoh 'made heavy' his heart (Exod 8:15, 8:32, 9:34). Also Rehoboam threatening to make the yoke heavier (1Kgs 12:10). Arabic athqala and Korean wangohage hada confirm the causative-negative dimension distinct from honoring.
senses.5: Nifal with divine subject: to be glorified, to get glory (13x). Predominantly God manifesting His glory through mighty acts. The Red Sea narrative is central: 'I will be glorified through Pharaoh' (Exod 14:4, 17, 18). Lev 10:3 ('before all the people I will be glorified') extends this to sanctuary contexts. French être-glorieux and German herrlich mark the theological register.
senses.6: Piel with God as object: to glorify, give glory to God (9x). The active worship counterpart of sense 5. Ps 86:9 ('all nations shall glorify your name'), Ps 22:23, Ps 50:15, 23. Arabic majjada, Korean yeonghwaropge hada, Swahili -tukuza all render divine glorification, confirming a distinct liturgical-doxological sense.
senses.7: Hitpael reflexive: to make oneself heavy, multiply oneself, or boast (4x). 2Chr 25:19 (Amaziah glorifying himself after victory), Prov 12:9 (one who honors himself vs. one who lacks bread), Nah 3:15 ('make yourself heavy as locusts' — multiply). French glorifier and Spanish glorificarte confirm the self-directed nature.
senses.8: Piel/Qal specifically of hardening the heart — making it unresponsive (3x). Exod 9:7 ('Pharaoh's heart was heavy'), 1Sam 6:6 ('why do you harden your hearts as Egypt hardened?'). This is metaphorical heaviness applied to the will, a subset of sense 2/4 that the multilingual evidence treats distinctly: French and German use harden rather than lourd/schwer.
senses.9: Stative/adjectival: to be rich, wealthy, abounding in possessions (2x). Gen 13:2 ('Abram was very rich in livestock') and Prov 8:24 ('springs abounding with water'). The semantic link is that 'heavy' in goods means wealthy — German war-sehr-reich confirms the economic reading. A natural metaphorical extension from physical mass to material abundance.
senses.10: Qal imperfect in jussive/optative sense: 'let the LORD be glorified' or 'may God be honored' (2x). Isa 66:5 and Job 14:21. This stative-passive use with glory semantics bridges senses 2 and 5 — the verb's weight becomes divine weight, i.e., glory. Distinct from Nifal sense 5 by its optative mood and Qal stem.
senses.11: Hifil with positive honorific sense: to bring honor to, make glorious (2x). Isa 9:1 ('he will make glorious the way of the sea') and Jer 30:19 ('I will honor them'). Unlike sense 4's negative Hifil (burden/harden), this causative produces honor and splendor. Spanish honrará and French honorer confirm the positive valence.
senses.12: 2Sam 13:25: 'Let us not all go, lest we burden you' — Absalom's diplomatic words to David. English 'burden' and Spanish carga show a social-logistical heaviness: the weight of hosting too many guests. A unique blend of physical heaviness (sense 2) applied to interpersonal obligation, classified under movement because of the travel context.

gloss_terse: To be good, pleasing, or glad; to do good, treat well, improve; to make merry or perform skillfully (Qal/Hifil)
gloss_readable: Rooted in the elemental concept of goodness, yatav moves fluidly between states and actions. In Qal, something 'is good' in someone's eyes or a heart 'is merry' with wine (Ruth 3:7). In Hifil, the subject actively does good, treats someone well, or improves a situation — God promises to 'do good' to Jacob (Gen 32:12) and Jeremiah urges Israel to 'make good' their ways (Jer 7:3). Arabic distinguishes hasuna ('be good') from ahsana ('do good') and aslaha ('make right'), mirroring Hebrew's own internal sense boundaries with remarkable precision.

senses.1: Hifil causative: to do good to someone, treat well, bestow benefit (42x). The dominant active sense. Arabic Form IV ahsana ('do good') confirms the causative structure. Gen 12:16 (Pharaoh treating Abram well for Sarai's sake), Gen 32:12 (God promising to 'do good'), and Deut 8:16 are foundational. Spanish hacer-bien and French faire-du-bien are consistent.
senses.2: Qal stative: to be good, be pleasing, go well with someone (38x). Impersonal constructions with le- dominate: 'it was good in his eyes' (Gen 41:37), 'it will go well with you' (Deut 4:40). Arabic hasuna ('be good/beautiful') and French cela-est-bon render the evaluative-stative meaning. Gen 34:18 ('the words were good') and Gen 45:16 ('the report was good') show propositional subjects.
senses.3: Hifil infinitive absolute used adverbially: well, thoroughly, clearly (10x). Functions as an intensifier modifying another verb — 'inquire well' (Deut 13:14), 'grind thoroughly' (Deut 9:21). Arabic jayyidan ('well') and the adverb entièrement in French confirm the adverbial function. The Deuteronomic legal corpus uses this form repeatedly to require diligent investigation (Deut 13:14, 17:4, 19:18).
senses.4: Hifil: to amend, improve, make right (7x). Concentrated in Jeremiah's reform preaching: 'Make good your ways and your deeds' (Jer 7:3, 5). Arabic crucially shifts to aslaha ('repair, reform') rather than ahsana ('do good'), confirming a distinct semantic field of correction rather than benefaction. Spanish mejorad ('improve') captures this precisely.
senses.5: Qal: to be glad, merry (of the heart or spirit) (5x). The internal-emotional dimension: a heart 'being good' means being joyful. Judg 19:6, 9 (a father-in-law's heart merry at feasting), Ruth 3:7 (Boaz's heart merry with wine). Arabic taba ('be pleasant/delightful') replaces hasuna here, revealing a genuine semantic distinction within the Qal itself.
senses.6: Prov 30:29–30: 'stately in stride' — describing animals that walk with impressive bearing. The sense of being fine, impressive, or stately in manner or movement. Spanish los-que-marchan-bien ('those who march well') and the repeated context of lions, roosters, and kings confirm a sense of dignified, admirable deportment unique to this wisdom passage.
senses.7: Hifil: to play or perform music skillfully (2x). Ps 33:3 ('play skillfully with a shout of joy') and Isa 23:16 ('play well, sing many songs'). Spanish tocad-bien ('play well') confirms the musical-technical sense. Arabic ahsinu retains the root meaning 'do well' but the collocation with instruments creates a specialized performance nuance.
senses.8: Hifil: to make merry, cause joy, cheer (2x). Judg 19:22 ('making merry') and Eccl 11:9 ('let your heart cheer you'). Arabic yusarruna (Form II of s-r-r, 'cause gladness') shifts entirely away from the goodness root, confirming this as a causative-emotional sense distinct from sense 1's benefaction. The heart is not just glad (sense 5) but is being made glad.
senses.9: 2Kgs 9:30: Jezebel 'adorned' or 'beautified' her eyes (with cosmetics). Spanish adornó and English adorned reveal a unique application of 'making good' to personal appearance — specifically applying eye-paint. The Hifil here means 'to make beautiful, adorn,' a concrete, cosmetic sense found only in this dramatic passage.
senses.10: Exod 30:7: Aaron 'tends' or 'trims' the lamps each morning. English 'tends' and Spanish aderezar point to a priestly-technical sense of making the lamps burn properly — 'making them good.' A cultic maintenance action: ensuring the lampstand functions well, unique to tabernacle/temple service vocabulary.
senses.11: Nah 3:8: 'Are you better situated than No-Amon (Thebes)?' — a comparative use where yatav means 'be better placed, be in a more advantageous position than.' Spanish eres-mejor and French faire-du-bien attempt the comparison. This is the Qal stative applied geopolitically: Nineveh's situation evaluated against fallen Thebes.
senses.12: 1Sam 20:13: 'If it seems good to my father' — an impersonal conditional use where the verb expresses approval or favorable disposition. Spanish si-pareciere-bien ('if it should seem good') captures the deliberative nuance. A specialized politeness formula within the broader 'be good/pleasing' sense (related to sense 2 but functioning as a diplomatic conditional).
